title: Terminates TPS for Nepal
description_short: DHS announced the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Nepal.
description_medium: On April 26, 2018, the Department of Homeland Security announced that Nepal’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end. TPS let eligible Nepali nationals already in the United States remain and work temporarily after the 2015 earthquake made safe return difficult. DHS set a transition period before the protection expired, so the announcement did not mean immediate deportation. It began the process of ending a humanitarian immigration status for people covered by the designation.
description_long: The Department of Homeland Security announced on April 26, 2018, that it would terminate Temporary Protected Status for Nepal. The designation had followed the 2015 earthquake, which left conditions that made safe return difficult for eligible Nepali nationals living in the United States. TPS allowed qualifying people to remain and work temporarily while the designation was active; it was not permanent residence or citizenship. DHS provided a transition period before the termination took effect. That gave people time to seek another lawful immigration status or prepare to leave, but it did not guarantee that either option would be available to every TPS holder. The announcement therefore changed the legal position of the covered group over time rather than ordering removals on the day it was issued. The decision was part of the administration’s review of country-specific TPS designations and drew attention to how humanitarian protections can be ended even when recipients have built lives in the United States. The policy affected Nepali nationals who qualified under the designation; it did not change the status of every person from Nepal.
subcategory: Legal Immigration Status Revocation and Humanitarian Protection Elimination

title: Sets Refugee Admissions Cap at 18,000
description_short: Issued a determination setting the FY2020 refugee admissions ceiling at 18,000.
description_medium: For fiscal year 2020, President Trump set the refugee admissions ceiling at 18,000 in a determination issued November 1, 2019. The ceiling was the maximum number the United States could admit through its resettlement program that year, not a promise that all 18,000 places would be filled. The cap continued a sharp reduction in refugee resettlement and limited the number of people who could be considered for admission.
description_long: On November 1, 2019, President Trump issued the determination setting the fiscal year 2020 refugee admissions ceiling at 18,000. The annual ceiling establishes the maximum number of refugees the United States may admit through its resettlement program during that fiscal year. It is not a guarantee that the full number will arrive: applicants still pass through eligibility screening, referrals, security checks, and travel arrangements. The 18,000 limit was described as a record low and marked a further contraction of the U.S. resettlement program. Refugees are people outside their country who cannot safely return because of persecution or other qualifying circumstances; resettlement offers a route to protection for a small share of those displaced worldwide. A lower ceiling narrows that route, even if the eventual admissions total falls below the cap for other reasons. The determination set the administration’s formal limit for FY2020 and left the agencies to conduct the individual selection and processing work within it. The figure describes authorized capacity, not the number ultimately admitted that year.
subcategory: Refugee and Asylum Protection System Elimination

title: Pardons Steve Bannon
description_short: Trump pardoned former adviser Steve Bannon in his final hours in office.
description_medium: On January 20, 2021, President Trump pardoned former adviser Steve Bannon in a final-day clemency announcement. Bannon had been charged in the federal We Build the Wall case, which concerned alleged fraud involving donations to a private fundraising effort. A pardon forgives covered federal offenses, unlike a commutation, which reduces a sentence. Trump’s action came before Bannon’s case went to trial.
description_long: President Trump included former adviser Steve Bannon in the clemency actions announced on January 20, 2021, his last day in office. Bannon had been charged in the federal We Build the Wall case over an alleged scheme to misuse donations raised for construction along the U.S.-Mexico border. He had pleaded not guilty, and his trial had not begun when Trump granted the pardon. A presidential pardon can forgive covered federal offenses, but it does not erase the historical record of charges or establish that the allegations were false. It is also distinct from a commutation, which changes a sentence after conviction without vacating the judgment. The final-day grant placed a former senior adviser among dozens of people who received clemency as Trump left office. Because the clemency action concerned federal authority, it could not resolve any separate state matter. The pardon drew scrutiny because Bannon had been a close political ally and was awaiting trial in a prominent fundraising case. The event was an exercise of presidential clemency before a jury could hear the federal allegations.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump pardoned former adviser Steve Bannon in his final hours in office.

title: Signs Executive Orders Targeting TikTok and WeChat
description_short: Signed executive orders banning U.S. transactions with ByteDance's TikTok and Tencent's WeChat.
description_medium: On August 6, 2020, Trump signed separate executive orders targeting transactions involving TikTok owner ByteDance and WeChat owner Tencent. The orders cited national security concerns and sought to restrict U.S. dealings with the companies, putting the apps’ availability and business operations at risk. The announcement began a legal and administrative dispute over the reach of executive power and the place of foreign-owned platforms in the U.S. market.
description_long: On August 6, 2020, President Trump signed two executive orders aimed at TikTok, owned by ByteDance, and WeChat, owned by Tencent. Both orders invoked national security and sought to prohibit specified U.S. transactions with the companies. The measures did not instantly remove either app from users’ phones; their practical effect depended on the transactions covered, implementing steps, and court review. The threatened restrictions put the platforms’ U.S. operations in doubt and raised questions about the government’s power to regulate communications services through emergency authorities. They also brought competing concerns into view: the administration’s security claims, the companies’ commercial interests, and the effects a broad restriction could have on users and speech. The orders were challenged in court, which complicated their implementation and kept the dispute from ending with the signing. The episode became an early example of the administration seeking to reshape the U.S. technology market through executive action directed at Chinese-owned companies. It records the orders and their stated targets; the signing alone did not mean that the proposed restrictions all took effect.

preserved_fields.title: Signs Executive Orders Targeting TikTok and WeChat
preserved_fields.description_short: Signed executive orders banning U.S. transactions with ByteDance's TikTok and Tencent's WeChat.

title: Issues “Buy American, Hire American” Order
description_short: Signed Executive Order 13788 directing agencies to tighten immigration and procurement rules.
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 13788, “Buy American and Hire American,” on April 18, 2017. It directed agencies to review federal procurement rules and immigration programs, including the H-1B visa system, with the stated aim of favoring U.S.-made goods and protecting domestic workers. The order launched agency reviews; changes to contracts and visa administration depended on later guidance and rulemaking.
description_long: Executive Order 13788, signed by President Trump on April 18, 2017, joined procurement and immigration policy under the slogan “Buy American and Hire American.” It instructed federal agencies to review how they purchased goods and services, with the stated goal of giving preference to products made in the United States. It also directed a review of immigration programs, including the H-1B visa system, to identify ways to protect U.S. workers. The order did not itself rewrite every procurement rule or change each visa decision. Agencies had to examine their existing authority and decide whether additional guidance, enforcement changes, or formal rulemaking was needed. Its immediate effect was to set those reviews in motion and establish the administration’s policy direction. The order connected trade and employment priorities in one executive action and put agencies under pressure to consider domestic preferences in purchasing and worker protections in visa administration. Any later economic or employment effects depended on the rules and decisions that followed, rather than on the signature alone.

title: Names Matthew Whitaker Acting Attorney General
description_short: Trump appointed Matthew Whitaker as acting attorney general immediately after Sessions’s resignation.
description_medium: After Jeff Sessions resigned as attorney general on November 7, 2018, Trump designated Matthew Whitaker to serve as acting attorney general. Whitaker had been Sessions’s chief of staff and had publicly criticized aspects of the special counsel investigation into Russian election interference. His appointment placed him over the Justice Department while that inquiry continued and prompted legal questions about his authority and potential role in its supervision.
description_long: On November 7, 2018, Jeff Sessions resigned as attorney general at Trump’s request, and the president designated Matthew Whitaker as acting attorney general. Whitaker had served as Sessions’s chief of staff and had previously made public comments critical of the special counsel investigation into Russian election interference. His appointment therefore raised immediate questions about who would oversee the inquiry and whether Whitaker could lawfully perform the attorney general’s duties under the succession rules. The investigation continued after the change in leadership, but the acting attorney general headed the department responsible for its operations and could potentially supervise matters involving the special counsel. Legal scholars and members of Congress disputed the appointment’s validity and raised concerns about Whitaker’s earlier comments. The appointment did not itself establish that he would interfere with the investigation, and it did not end the inquiry. It did, however, place a politically appointed official who had expressed skepticism about the probe in a position of departmental authority while the investigation remained active. That overlap made the succession decision consequential beyond an ordinary leadership change.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jennings Gilbert
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jennings Gilbert as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: President Trump commuted Jennings Gilbert’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021, as part of a late-term clemency list. The Justice Department records a 240-month prison term and ten years of supervised release for a marijuana manufacturing and distribution conspiracy involving more than 1,000 plants. A commutation changes punishment without overturning the conviction; the public clemency entry does not specify which sentence terms Trump reduced.
description_long: President Trump commuted Jennings Gilbert’s sentence on January 19, 2021, one day before leaving office. The Justice Department’s clemency list records that Gilbert was sentenced in 2006 to 240 months in prison followed by ten years of supervised release. The listed case involved a conspiracy to manufacture more than 1,000 marijuana plants and possession with intent to distribute. A commutation reduces or otherwise changes punishment but leaves the conviction in place; it is different from a pardon and does not amount to a judicial finding that the case was wrongly decided. Gilbert received clemency as part of a group of actions announced near the end of Trump’s term. The published listing identifies the original sentence and the grant, but does not describe the terms of the commutation or explain the president’s choice. The decision shortened the consequences imposed by the federal judgment to the extent specified in the clemency instrument. It did not erase the underlying conviction or convert the federal case into an acquittal.

title: YouTube Suspends Trump Channel and Disables Comments
description_short: YouTube suspended Trump’s channel and disabled comments after violations related to incitement concerns.
description_medium: YouTube suspended Trump’s channel from uploading videos and disabled comments on January 12, 2021. The company said recent content violated its policies and that it acted amid concern about further incitement after the January 6 attack on the Capitol. The restriction followed similar steps by other platforms. It was a private company’s enforcement decision, not a government order, and initially left open the possibility of later review.
description_long: YouTube announced on January 12, 2021, that Trump’s channel could no longer upload new videos and that comments had been disabled. The company said it removed content for violating its policies and cited the risk of further incitement after the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The restriction came as social media companies reassessed how Trump’s accounts could be used in the aftermath of the attack. It was a private platform’s enforcement decision under its own rules, not a government order barring the former president from speaking. YouTube initially described the action as a suspension while it reviewed the risk and its policies, rather than a permanent removal announced that day. The decision limited Trump’s ability to post video on one major platform during the transition out of office, while leaving other channels available to him. It also highlighted the influence private platforms held over access to large online audiences and the controversy around how they should respond to political speech linked to real-world violence.

title: Ends ACA Cost-Sharing Reduction Payments
description_short: The administration stopped federal CSR payments to insurers under the Affordable Care Act.
description_medium: The Trump administration ended federal cost-sharing reduction payments to insurers on October 12, 2017. Under the Affordable Care Act, those payments reimbursed insurers for lowering deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs for eligible low-income customers. The legal requirement to provide the reductions remained, shifting the cost onto insurers and prompting responses such as higher premiums. The decision created immediate uncertainty for insurers and state regulators.
description_long: On October 12, 2017, the Trump administration announced it would stop reimbursing health insurers for cost-sharing reductions under the Affordable Care Act. The payments supported lower deductibles, copayments, and other out-of-pocket charges for eligible low-income enrollees who bought certain marketplace plans. The ACA requirement that insurers provide those reductions remained in force, so ending the federal payments did not remove the benefit from eligible customers. Instead, insurers had to account for the lost reimbursement when setting premiums and deciding which plans to offer. Some states and insurers responded by adding the cost to premiums for marketplace plans, a practice known as silver loading; the exact effects varied by state and plan. The decision followed the administration’s broader effort to reduce federal support for ACA implementation. It shifted a financing obligation and forced state insurance regulators to address uncertainty ahead of future enrollment periods. The payment termination was an administrative policy change, not a repeal of the ACA or an immediate cancellation of cost-sharing assistance.
subcategory: Social Safety Net Destruction and Vulnerable Population Abandonment

title: House Impeaches Trump for Incitement of Insurrection
description_short: The House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection following the Jan. 6 attack.
description_medium: The House of Representatives impeached Donald Trump on January 13, 2021, charging him with “incitement of insurrection” after the January 6 attack on the Capitol. The House approved one article with bipartisan support, making Trump the first president impeached twice. Impeachment is a formal charge, not removal from office or a criminal conviction. The Senate later held a trial and acquitted him.
description_long: On January 13, 2021, the House of Representatives approved one article of impeachment charging President Donald Trump with “incitement of insurrection” after a mob attacked the U.S. Capitol on January 6. The vote included support from members of both parties and made Trump the first U.S. president impeached twice. The House’s action formally accused him of misconduct; impeachment alone does not convict a president or remove him from office. The Senate is responsible for conducting the trial and deciding whether to convict. It later acquitted Trump, so the House vote did not result in a Senate conviction. The impeachment followed the disruption of Congress as lawmakers met to count electoral votes from the 2020 election. The charge centered on Trump’s conduct before and during the attack, while criminal cases against individual rioters proceeded separately through the courts. The House vote therefore added a constitutional accountability proceeding to the aftermath of January 6, with the Senate’s later decision completing the process.
subcategory: Violent Government Overthrow and Constitutional Insurrection

title: Issues ACA Sabotage Executive Order
description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13765 directing agencies to minimize enforcement of ACA provisions.
description_medium: On January 20, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13765, directing agencies to use their legal discretion to reduce the Affordable Care Act’s regulatory and financial burdens while Congress considered repeal. Agencies were told to waive or delay requirements where the law allowed and to minimize enforcement. The order did not repeal the statute or automatically cancel insurance coverage; its effects depended on later agency decisions.
description_long: President Trump’s first executive order, signed January 20, 2017, instructed federal agencies to use authority available under existing law to reduce the Affordable Care Act’s regulatory and financial burdens. Executive Order 13765 directed agencies to waive, defer, or grant exemptions from requirements where legally permissible and to minimize enforcement while Congress considered repeal. The order did not itself repeal the ACA, which remained federal law, and it did not automatically cancel insurance coverage or end programs established by the statute. Its practical consequences depended on subsequent agency decisions and on what each agency had legal authority to change. By issuing the directive on his first day in office, Trump signaled that his administration would use executive discretion to weaken implementation while pursuing legislative repeal. The order initiated that administrative approach, but the effect on insurers, states, and people enrolled in coverage turned on the specific rules and actions that followed. It was an early test of how far the executive branch could alter the law’s operation without Congress changing the statute itself.
subcategory: Social Safety Net Destruction and Vulnerable Population Abandonment

title: Vetoes Yemen War Powers Resolution
description_short: Trump vetoed a bipartisan resolution to end U.S. involvement in the Yemen war.
description_medium: Trump vetoed a bipartisan resolution on April 16, 2019, that sought to end U.S. support for the Saudi-led campaign in Yemen under the War Powers Resolution. Congress had used the measure to challenge military assistance and other backing for the coalition. The veto stopped the resolution from taking effect unless lawmakers could override it, preserving the administration’s policy at that point.
description_long: On April 16, 2019, President Trump vetoed a bipartisan congressional resolution that would have directed the removal of U.S. forces from unauthorized hostilities in Yemen. Congress had invoked the War Powers Resolution to challenge U.S. support for the Saudi-led coalition, including assistance and logistical backing for its military campaign. The veto prevented the resolution from becoming law unless Congress could override it with a two-thirds vote in each chamber. Trump’s action rejected Congress’s effort to use the statute to constrain the administration’s role in the conflict and allowed its support policy to continue at that time. The veto did not declare war or resolve every question about the limits of presidential authority in future operations. It instead kept this specific congressional measure from taking effect. The dispute reflected a broader tension over who controls U.S. military involvement abroad: the president directing foreign policy and Congress exercising its constitutional powers over war and funding. The veto preserved the administration’s position while leaving the underlying debate over Yemen and war powers unresolved.

title: Commutes Sentence of Sholom Rubashkin
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Sholom Rubashkin as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Sholom Rubashkin’s federal prison sentence on December 20, 2017, reducing a 27-year term after he had served about eight years. The Justice Department lists convictions for bank fraud, false statements, wire fraud, mail fraud, and money laundering connected to his meatpacking business, along with more than $26.8 million in restitution. A commutation changes the sentence but leaves the convictions in place.
description_long: President Trump commuted Sholom Rubashkin’s sentence on December 20, 2017, reducing a 27-year federal prison term imposed in 2010. Rubashkin had served about eight years. The Justice Department’s clemency record lists bank fraud, false statements to a bank, wire fraud, mail fraud, and money laundering among the convictions, along with more than $26.8 million in restitution. A commutation shortens or changes punishment but does not vacate the convictions, as a pardon may, or reverse the court’s judgment. The clemency decision therefore reduced the prison sentence while leaving the underlying case and its restitution order on the record. It drew attention because the offenses involved a large financial fraud at a meatpacking business and because the reduction cut many years from the original term. The public record documents the sentence relief and the case background; the commutation itself was an act of presidential clemency, not a judicial finding that the prosecution or conviction was invalid.
